direct_observables: ion current (intensity) at specific mass-to-charge ratio (m/z)
derived_observables: partial vapor pressures (from calibrated ion intensities)
total vapor pressure (sum of partial pressures of all gaseous species)
enthalpy of sublimation (from Clausius-Clapeyron analysis of ln(p) vs. 1/T)
enthalpy of vaporization (from temperature-dependent vapor pressure data)
thermodynamic equilibrium constants for gas-phase reactions
target_properties: partial pressures of individual gaseous species over condensed phases
phases_measured: solid (indirectly, via equilibrium vapor over solid sample)
liquid (indirectly, via equilibrium vapor over liquid sample)
supported_sample_types: low-volatility inorganic compounds (metal oxides, halides, chalcogenides)
unsupported_sample_types: highly volatile liquids with vapor pressures > 1 Pa at room temperature (overwhelm the effusion regime)
gases (no condensed phase to establish Knudsen equilibrium)
thermally unstable compounds that decompose before producing measurable vapor
samples that react aggressively with Knudsen cell materials (alumina, platinum, graphite)
large-volume liquid samples requiring continuous flow introduction
typical_output_formats: mass spectrum (ion intensity vs. m/z) at fixed cell temperature
ion intensity vs. temperature curve for selected m/z (vaporization curve)
partial vapor pressure vs. temperature table

constraints.hard_limits: lower limit set by detectable vapor pressure (~10⁻⁷ Pa); upper limit set by cell material stability (alumina ~2100 K, tungsten ~2800 K)
constraints.notes: temperature must be sufficient to produce equilibrium vapor pressure in the molecular flow regime

constraints.hard_limits: orifice must be small enough that the Clausing factor is well-defined and molecular flow (Knudsen number > 10) is maintained
constraints.notes: larger orifices increase signal but risk depleting the condensed phase and violating equilibrium; orifice area/evaporation area ratio (Whitman-Motzfeldt correction) matters

constraints.hard_limits: must exceed ionization potential of analyte species (~5–15 eV); standard setting is 70 eV for reproducible fragmentation
constraints.notes: lower energies (appearance potential measurements) reduce fragmentation but decrease sensitivity

constraints.hard_limits: must maintain molecular flow conditions; residual gas background must be low enough to distinguish analyte ions
constraints.notes: differential pumping between Knudsen cell chamber and analyzer improves signal-to-background

variables.name: Knudsen_cell_temperature
variables.effect: determines equilibrium vapor pressure; temperature scanning yields enthalpy of sublimation/vaporization from van 't Hoff analysis

variables.name: electron_energy
variables.effect: controls fragmentation extent and ionization probability; 70 eV is standard for quantitative work; lower energies used for appearance potential measurements

variables.name: sample_composition
variables.typical_values: binary alloy compositions across full mole fraction range
variables.effect: partial pressures of components vary with composition, enabling determination of activity coefficients and excess Gibbs energies

variables.name: pressure
variables.effect: vapor pressure is the primary thermodynamic quantity derived from ion intensities; must remain in molecular flow regime

instrument_components: Knudsen effusion cell — isothermal enclosure (alumina, graphite, platinum, molybdenum, or tungsten crucible with calibrated orifice) containing the sample at thermodynamic equilibrium
resistive or induction furnace — heats the Knudsen cell to the target temperature with stability ±0.5 K or better
temperature measurement system — Type B, S, or C thermocouple or optical pyrometer positioned at the cell wall or base
molecular beam collimator/shutter — defines the effusing molecular beam and allows background subtraction via beam chopping
electron ionization source — electron gun producing a well-defined electron beam (typically 70 eV) that ionizes the effusate
mass analyzer — magnetic sector or quadrupole mass filter separating ions by m/z ratio
ion detector — secondary electron multiplier (SEM) or Faraday cup for measuring ion currents
vacuum system — turbomolecular and/or diffusion pumps maintaining 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁵ Pa in the ion source and analyzer regions
data acquisition and control system — computer interface for temperature programming, mass scanning, and ion current recording
environmental_requirements: high vacuum (< 10⁻⁵ Pa) in the entire flight path from Knudsen cell to detector
differential pumping between cell chamber and ion source to reduce background gas interference
water cooling for vacuum chamber walls and furnace surroundings
vibration isolation to prevent misalignment of molecular beam and ion optics
clean vacuum (low hydrocarbon background) achieved by baking and use of oil-free pumps where possible

geometry: powder (most common — maximizes surface area for rapid equilibration)
sample_requirements.size_limits: typically 10–500 mg; must be sufficient to maintain a condensed phase throughout the measurement but not so large as to produce excessive thermal gradients
sample_requirements.thickness_limits: not critical for powders; for solid pieces, should be small enough to achieve thermal equilibrium with the cell within the dwell time at each temperature
surface_requirements: clean surface free of volatile contaminants (grease, adsorbed gases)
oxide layers on metals should be removed or accounted for in initial conditioning runs
mounting_requirements: sample placed inside the Knudsen cell crucible without blocking the orifice
for alloy studies, sample should be pre-alloyed to the target composition
cell lid with orifice must seal properly to prevent effusion from gaps
preparation_requirements: pre-drying and degassing under vacuum before measurement
initial conditioning run to remove surface contaminants and volatile impurities (first temperature ramp data typically discarded)
verification of sample purity by independent analysis (e.g., elemental analysis, XRD)
for alloy systems, confirmation of phase homogeneity before effusion measurement

calibration_requirements: pressure calibration using a reference substance with well-known vapor pressure (silver, gold, or zinc) to determine the instrument sensitivity constant k in p = k·I·T/σ
temperature calibration against melting points of certified reference metals (e.g., Au at 1337.33 K, Ag at 1234.93 K, Cu at 1357.77 K)
ionization cross-section calibration — relative or absolute σ values for each gaseous species, either measured or taken from literature
mass discrimination calibration — correction for m/z-dependent transmission efficiency of the mass analyzer and detector
Clausing factor determination for the specific orifice geometry (analytical or Monte Carlo calculation)
reference_materials: silver — primary vapor pressure standard (well-characterized thermodynamic data from NIST/JANAF)
gold — vapor pressure standard for high-temperature work
zinc — lower-temperature vapor pressure reference (useful 600–1000 K range)
naphthalene or anthracene — organic vapor pressure standards for moderate temperature range
consumables: Knudsen cell crucibles (alumina, graphite, platinum, molybdenum, tungsten — material chosen for chemical inertness with sample)
cell orifice lids (precision-machined with known orifice diameter)
thermocouples (Type B, S, or C depending on temperature range)
electron filaments for the ionization source (tungsten or rhenium)
secondary electron multiplier (periodic replacement due to gain degradation)
safety_notes: high vacuum systems require implosion protection and proper venting procedures
high-temperature furnaces (> 1500 K) pose severe burn risk; appropriate shielding and interlocks required
some samples (e.g., metal halides, chalcogenides) may release toxic vapors — fume hood or enclosed systems required for sample preparation
high-voltage supplies for electron gun and SEM detector require standard electrical safety precautions
radioactive or highly toxic samples require specialized containment cells and regulatory compliance

performance.sensitivity: detectable partial pressures as low as ~10⁻⁷ Pa (SEM detection); ~10⁻⁴ Pa for Faraday cup detection; corresponds to ion currents in the fA to pA range for SEM
performance.detection_limit: minimum sample vapor pressure ~10⁻⁷ Pa with SEM; ~10⁻⁴ Pa with Faraday cup; sample mass as low as ~5 mg for short experiments

resolution.temporal: limited by mass scan speed and temperature equilibration; typical dwell time 1–10 s per m/z channel; full temperature equilibration 5–30 min per step
resolution.spectral: unit mass resolution (Δm = 1 amu) for quadrupole analyzers; m/Δm ~ 500–5000 for magnetic sector instruments
resolution.energy: electron energy resolution ~0.5–1 eV for appearance potential measurements

performance.dynamic_range: ion current dynamic range ~10⁶ (fA to µA); vapor pressure range ~10⁻⁷ Pa to ~10 Pa within molecular flow regime
performance.accuracy: 5–20% for absolute vapor pressures (dominated by ionization cross-section and calibration uncertainties); ±2–5 kJ/mol for enthalpy of sublimation by second-law method; ±1–3 kJ/mol for third-law method when reliable thermodynamic functions are available
performance.precision: 2–5% (repeatability of ion intensity ratios at a given temperature); enthalpy precision ±1–2 kJ/mol from repeated experiments
performance.throughput: single sample per run; complete vapor pressure vs. temperature dataset typically requires 4–12 hours per sample depending on temperature range and number of points
performance.measurement_speed: individual ion intensity measurement is fast (seconds); rate-limiting step is thermal equilibration of Knudsen cell at each temperature step (5–30 min)

data_and_interpretation.raw_signal_type: ion current at each m/z value as a function of Knudsen cell temperature, recorded as amperes (A) from SEM or Faraday cup detector; background-subtracted by beam shutter cycling (shutter open minus shutter closed)
preprocessing_steps: background subtraction using shutter-closed baseline at each m/z to remove residual gas contributions
correction for detector gain (SEM multiplier gain calibration) and mass discrimination
isotope deconvolution to separate overlapping peaks from different species at the same nominal m/z
fragmentation correction — reassignment of fragment ion intensities to parent molecular species using known cracking patterns
baseline drift correction for slow changes in electron emission current or detector gain
analysis_methods: Hertz-Knudsen equation: p = k·I·T/σ, where k is the instrument sensitivity constant, I is ion intensity, T is cell temperature, and σ is the ionization cross-section
second-law (van 't Hoff) method: ΔsubH° = −R·d[ln(I·T)]/d(1/T) from slope of ln(I·T) vs. 1/T plot
third-law method: ΔsubH°(298 K) = T·[−R·ln(Kp) + Δ(G°−H°298)/T] evaluated at each experimental temperature using tabulated thermodynamic functions
Whitman-Motzfeldt correction for non-ideal orifice geometry (finite Clausing factor)
multi-species equilibrium analysis for systems with several gaseous species (e.g., dissociative vaporization)
model_assumptions: thermodynamic equilibrium is established between the condensed phase and the vapor inside the Knudsen cell
molecular flow (Knudsen regime) through the orifice — mean free path >> orifice diameter
effusion through the orifice does not perturb the equilibrium significantly (orifice area << evaporation surface area)
ionization cross-sections are independent of temperature (valid for electron impact at 70 eV)
gaseous species behave as ideal gases at the low pressures involved
no significant chemical reaction between the sample and the cell material
fit_parameters: instrument sensitivity constant k (determined from calibrant with known vapor pressure)
enthalpy of sublimation/vaporization ΔH (from slope of van 't Hoff plot)
entropy of sublimation/vaporization ΔS (from intercept of van 't Hoff plot)
ionization cross-section σ for each gaseous species (from literature or relative calibration)
Clausing factor W for the specific orifice geometry
common_artifacts: surface desorption transient — initial high ion intensities from adsorbed gases on cell walls and sample surface that decay over time
cell-sample reaction — formation of volatile reaction products (e.g., metal carbides from graphite cells) that contaminate the mass spectrum
non-equilibrium effusion — if heating rate is too fast or sample surface area is too small, the vapor inside the cell is not in equilibrium with the condensed phase
fragmentation pattern changes — apparent changes in cracking pattern with temperature if ion source geometry shifts thermally
memory effect — residual vapor from a previous sample coating the cell interior and producing ghost signals
multiple orifice flow — leaks in the cell seal create uncontrolled effusion paths
quality_control_checks: verify equilibrium: check that ion intensities are reproducible on heating and cooling cycles
measure a reference substance (silver or gold) to confirm the instrument sensitivity constant agrees with literature vapor pressure
check linearity of ln(I·T) vs. 1/T plot — deviations indicate phase transitions, decomposition, or loss of equilibrium
compare second-law and third-law enthalpies — agreement within ±3 kJ/mol indicates self-consistent data
monitor total ion current stability at constant temperature to verify no sample depletion or cell degradation
verify orifice is not clogged by condensation of low-volatility products
failure_modes: Knudsen cell cracking or orifice blockage from sample creep, sintering, or condensation of involatile products
cell-sample reaction forming carbides, oxides, or intermetallics that contaminate results and destroy the cell
thermocouple failure or decalibration at high temperatures, leading to systematic temperature error
electron filament burnout in the ionization source, requiring source disassembly and filament replacement
SEM detector gain degradation producing a slow decline in apparent ion intensities over the course of the experiment
sample depletion — insufficient condensed phase remaining to maintain equilibrium vapor pressure

uncertainty.level: typical combined standard uncertainty 5–20% for absolute vapor pressures; ±2–5 kJ/mol for enthalpy of sublimation (second-law); ±1–3 kJ/mol (third-law with reliable thermodynamic functions)
random_sources: ion counting statistics (Poisson noise) — dominant at low ion intensities
temperature fluctuations of the Knudsen cell (±0.5–2 K)
systematic_sources: ionization cross-section uncertainty (typically ±20–50% for absolute values; ±5–10% for relative values)
instrument sensitivity constant calibration (depends on reference substance vapor pressure accuracy)
temperature measurement offset or drift (thermocouple calibration, cold-junction compensation)
Clausing factor uncertainty for non-ideal orifice geometries
mass discrimination correction in the analyzer and detector
fragmentation pattern assignment errors — misattribution of fragment ions to wrong parent species
non-equilibrium effusion if sample vaporization kinetics are slow relative to effusion rate
uncertainty.operator_dependence: moderate to high — results depend on cell preparation (orifice quality, sample loading), temperature calibration care, choice of ionization cross-sections, and judgment in excluding non-equilibrium data points
uncertainty.model_dependence: moderate — second-law enthalpies depend on the linearity assumption of the van 't Hoff plot and are sensitive to the chosen temperature range; third-law method depends on the accuracy of tabulated thermodynamic functions (heat capacity, entropy) for both condensed and gaseous phases
dominant_error_sources: ionization cross-section uncertainty (largest single contributor to absolute pressure error)
temperature measurement accuracy (a 2 K error at 1500 K shifts the enthalpy by ~1–2 kJ/mol)
instrument sensitivity constant calibration (propagates directly to pressure)
reported_as: combined expanded uncertainty U(p) at 95% confidence (k=2) for vapor pressures
standard uncertainty of enthalpy u(ΔsubH°) in kJ/mol
relative standard uncertainty as percentage for vapor pressures
comparison of second-law and third-law enthalpy values as internal consistency check

description_block.technique_overview: Mass spectrometry as applied in ThermoML refers primarily to Knudsen effusion mass spectrometry (KEMS), a technique that determines vapor pressures and thermochemical properties of low-volatility substances by analyzing the molecular beam effusing from a Knudsen cell. The effusate is ionized by electron impact and mass-analyzed, with ion intensities proportional to the partial pressures of individual gaseous species above the condensed sample. KEMS is one of the few methods capable of measuring absolute vapor pressures below 1 Pa and simultaneously identifying the composition of the vapor phase, making it indispensable for characterizing refractory materials, metal alloys, ionic liquids, and other systems with very low vapor pressures. In the ThermoML database, mass spectrometry data appear in the ActivityFugacityOsmoticProp group, reflecting its use for determining activity coefficients and related equilibrium quantities from partial pressure measurements over multicomponent systems.
description_block.how_it_operates: A weighed sample is placed inside a Knudsen effusion cell — a small isothermal crucible (alumina, graphite, or refractory metal) fitted with a precision orifice typically 0.3–2 mm in diameter. The cell is heated in high vacuum by a resistive or induction furnace to a temperature where the sample produces a measurable equilibrium vapor. Gaseous molecules effuse through the orifice as a directional molecular beam, which is collimated and directed into an electron ionization source operating at a fixed electron energy (typically 70 eV). The ionized species are separated by mass-to-charge ratio in a magnetic sector or quadrupole mass analyzer and detected by a secondary electron multiplier (SEM) or Faraday cup. A mechanical shutter between the cell and the ion source is cycled to allow background subtraction (shutter-closed signal subtracted from shutter-open signal). The cell temperature is stepped through a series of set points, and at each temperature the ion intensities of all relevant m/z peaks are recorded after thermal equilibration. The resulting ion intensity vs. temperature dataset is the primary raw output from which vapor pressures and enthalpies are derived.
description_block.core_theory: The Hertz-Knudsen equation relates the equilibrium vapor pressure p of a species to the molecular effusion rate through the cell orifice: p = (I·T)·k/σ, where I is the measured ion intensity at the detector, T is the absolute cell temperature, σ is the electron-impact ionization cross-section of the species, and k is the instrument sensitivity constant determined by calibration with a substance of known vapor pressure. The sensitivity constant k encapsulates the orifice Clausing factor, molecular beam geometry, ion source efficiency, mass analyzer transmission, and detector gain. For temperature-dependent studies, the enthalpy of sublimation is extracted by the second-law (van 't Hoff) method: plotting ln(I·T) versus 1/T yields a line whose slope equals −ΔsubH°/R. The more rigorous third-law method evaluates the enthalpy at a reference temperature (usually 298.15 K) at each experimental point using tabulated standard Gibbs energy functions, providing a consistency check against the second-law result. Agreement between second-law and third-law values within ±3 kJ/mol is generally accepted as confirmation of thermodynamic equilibrium and data self-consistency.
description_block.setup: A typical KEMS apparatus consists of a Knudsen cell mounted inside a vacuum furnace (resistive heating to ~2500 K or induction heating for higher temperatures), surrounded by radiation shields, and housed in a high-vacuum chamber pumped by turbomolecular pumps to a base pressure below 10⁻⁵ Pa. The cell temperature is measured by a thermocouple (Type B: Pt-Rh/Pt-Rh for 600–2000 K; Type C: W-Re for > 2000 K) positioned at the cell wall or base. A collimating slit assembly and mechanical chopper/shutter define the molecular beam path between the cell orifice and the electron ionization source. The ion source uses a heated tungsten or rhenium filament to produce a collimated electron beam that intersects the molecular beam at right angles. Ions are extracted, focused by electrostatic ion optics, and sorted by a magnetic sector (for high resolution and sensitivity) or quadrupole mass filter (for speed and flexibility). The detector is typically an SEM operating in analog current mode, with a Faraday cup available for high-intensity ions. The entire system is computer-controlled for temperature programming, mass scanning, shutter cycling, and data logging.
description_block.suitable_for: KEMS is uniquely suited for measuring vapor pressures of substances with very low volatility — metals, alloys, refractory oxides, carbides, nitrides, halides, and chalcogenides in the range 10⁻⁷ to 10 Pa. It excels at systems where multiple gaseous species are present simultaneously (dissociative or congruent vaporization), because the mass analyzer identifies each species individually. The technique is widely used for determining enthalpies of sublimation and vaporization of organometallic compounds, ionic liquids, and high-boiling organic molecules that are difficult to study by conventional ebulliometric or static methods. For multicomponent condensed phases (alloys, salt mixtures, slags), KEMS provides partial pressures of each component as a function of composition, enabling direct determination of activity coefficients, excess Gibbs energies, and mixing enthalpies. It is the method of choice when speciation of the vapor phase is needed alongside thermodynamic data.
description_block.core_limitations: The technique is destructive — the sample is consumed during effusion, and sufficient material must remain throughout the measurement to maintain an equilibrium condensed phase. Absolute vapor pressure accuracy is typically limited to 5–20% due to the cumulative uncertainties in ionization cross-sections, the instrument sensitivity constant, and the orifice Clausing factor. The molecular flow requirement restricts measurable pressures to below approximately 10 Pa; at higher pressures, the transition to viscous flow invalidates the Hertz-Knudsen equation. Measurement throughput is low: thorough equilibration at each temperature step, combined with the need for conditioning runs and calibrant runs, means that a complete dataset for one sample may require a full day or more of instrument time. Interactions between the sample and cell material (e.g., carbide formation with graphite crucibles, alloying with metal crucibles) can corrupt data and require careful cell material selection. The technique cannot be applied to highly volatile substances or gases, and appearance potential measurements for ionization energies require specialized low-energy electron optics not available on all instruments.
description_block.sample_preparation: Samples are typically prepared as fine powders or small solid pieces, weighed on an analytical balance (±0.01 mg), and loaded into the Knudsen cell crucible. The cell material must be chemically inert with respect to the sample at all measurement temperatures — alumina is the default for most oxides and moderate-temperature studies, graphite for metals and carbon-tolerant systems, platinum or tungsten for aggressive samples. Before measurement, the loaded cell is placed in the vacuum chamber and degassed at a moderate temperature (below the intended measurement range) for several hours to remove adsorbed water, gases, and volatile contaminants. An initial conditioning run (first heating ramp) is performed and its data discarded, as surface impurities and non-equilibrium desorption produce spurious signals. For alloy studies, samples are pre-alloyed by arc melting or induction melting to the desired composition, annealed for homogenization, and characterized by XRD or SEM/EDS before loading. Sample mass should be sufficient to sustain effusion throughout the full temperature program without complete vaporization.
description_block.calibration_and_references: Pressure calibration is the most critical step and involves measuring the ion intensity of a reference substance with well-established vapor pressure data under identical instrument conditions. Silver is the most widely used primary calibrant (using the NIST/JANAF recommended vapor pressure equation), applicable from ~1100 K to ~1600 K. Gold and zinc serve as alternatives for different temperature ranges. The calibrant is measured in the same type of Knudsen cell and under the same operating parameters as the unknown sample, and the instrument sensitivity constant k is computed by equating the measured I·T product to the known vapor pressure via the Hertz-Knudsen relation. Temperature is calibrated against the melting points of high-purity reference metals (Au, Ag, Cu, Ni). Ionization cross-sections for the gaseous species of interest are taken from literature compilations (e.g., the tables of Mann, Deutsch-Märk, or NIST Electron-Impact Cross Section Database) or determined by comparing ion intensities with those of a species of known cross-section. The calibration should be repeated periodically and whenever the ion source filament is replaced or the detector gain changes significantly.
description_block.data_interpretation: The primary data are ion current values I(T) at each m/z ratio as a function of cell temperature. After background subtraction (shutter correction) and fragmentation pattern analysis, each m/z peak is assigned to a gaseous parent species. Ion intensities are converted to partial vapor pressures using p = k·I·T/σ, with the sensitivity constant k from the calibrant and ionization cross-section σ from literature or calibration. For enthalpy determination by the second-law method, ln(I·T) is plotted against 1/T and the enthalpy is obtained from the weighted linear regression slope: ΔsubH° = −R × slope. The third-law method provides the enthalpy at 298.15 K at each temperature point by combining the measured equilibrium constant Kp with tabulated Gibbs energy functions: ΔsubH°(298 K) = T × [ΔfefT − R·ln(Kp)], where ΔfefT is the change in the free energy function. A constant third-law enthalpy across all temperatures indicates self-consistent data. For multicomponent systems, activity coefficients are derived from the ratio of partial pressures over the mixture to those over the pure components at the same temperature.
description_block.common_pitfalls: The most frequent pitfall is failure to achieve true thermodynamic equilibrium inside the Knudsen cell, which occurs when the vaporization rate from the condensed surface is too slow relative to the effusion rate through the orifice. This can be detected by systematically varying the orifice size (the vapor pressure must be independent of orifice area if equilibrium holds) or by checking reproducibility on heating vs. cooling. Using inappropriate cell materials leads to sample-cell reactions that create volatile byproducts, change the sample composition, and produce misleading mass spectra — this is especially problematic for metals in graphite cells (carbide formation) and for oxides in molybdenum cells (reduction). Neglecting to perform adequate conditioning runs results in contamination of early data points by surface-adsorbed species. Applying a single set of ionization cross-sections to all temperatures without verifying their temperature independence introduces systematic error. Finally, overlooking fragmentation overlap — where fragment ions from one species have the same nominal m/z as the molecular ion of another — leads to incorrect species identification and erroneous partial pressure assignments.
description_block.artifacts_and_failure_modes: Surface desorption transients appear as anomalously high ion intensities during the first heating ramp, decaying exponentially as adsorbed contaminants are depleted. Cell-sample reactions manifest as new, unexpected m/z peaks (e.g., CO or CO₂ from carbon-containing cells reacting with oxides) or as a progressive shift in the apparent vapor pressure over time at constant temperature. Orifice clogging due to sample creep, sintering, or condensation of involatile decomposition products is indicated by a sudden drop in all ion intensities. Memory effects from previous samples coating the cell interior produce spurious low-intensity peaks that do not follow the expected temperature dependence. Thermocouple decalibration at high temperatures causes systematic errors in reported temperature (and consequently in derived enthalpy values) — this can be caught by re-checking a melting point standard after the experiment. SEM gain degradation produces a slow, monotonic decline in all ion intensities over time that mimics a decrease in vapor pressure; periodic gain checks against a stable reference signal are essential.
description_block.reporting_checklist: Published KEMS results should include: Knudsen cell material and orifice diameter (with Clausing factor), temperature measurement method and calibration procedure, electron ionization energy, mass analyzer type and resolution, detector type, calibration reference substance and its vapor pressure equation, ionization cross-sections used (with literature source), raw ion intensity data or at minimum a table of derived vapor pressures vs. temperature, second-law and third-law enthalpy values with stated uncertainties, evidence of equilibrium (e.g., heating/cooling reproducibility, orifice size independence), description of fragmentation pattern corrections applied, sample purity and preparation method, and combined expanded uncertainty at 95% confidence level. For ThermoML encoding, activity coefficients and derived thermodynamic quantities are reported with nCombExpandUncertValue at the 95% confidence level.
